name: Heart rate
whyItMatters: Your resting heart rate shows how hard your heart works at rest. A lasting rise above your own baseline is worth a closer look.
howToMeasure: Read it from your wearable after waking, before you get up.

watch.text: Repeat the reading at rest tomorrow morning and compare it with your baseline.

alert.text: Repeat the reading at rest now. If it stays this high, follow the mission medical protocol.

name: Sleep
whyItMatters: NASA lists sleep loss and circadian desynchronization as a risk to crew performance and health.
howToMeasure: Hours asleep last night, from your wearable's actigraphy.

watch.text: Protect tonight's sleep period and review your light therapy schedule.

alert.text: Make sleep the priority for the next days and adjust your light therapy schedule.

name: Heart rate variability
whyItMatters: Heart rate variability reflects how well your body is recovering. A lasting drop below your own baseline is worth a closer look.
howToMeasure: Read the overnight value from your wearable.

watch.text: Check your sleep and workload for the last days; both can lower this value.

alert.text: Lighten today's workload if the plan allows it and follow the mission medical protocol.

name: Blood oxygen
whyItMatters: Blood oxygen depends on your lungs and on the air in the cabin. A lasting drop below your own baseline is worth a closer look.
howToMeasure: Use the finger sensor while sitting still.

watch.text: Repeat the reading while sitting still and check the cabin CO2 tile.

alert.text: Repeat the reading now. If it stays this low, follow the mission medical protocol.

name: Skin temperature
whyItMatters: Skin temperature follows your daily rhythm and the cabin climate. A lasting shift from your own baseline is worth a closer look.
howToMeasure: Read the overnight value from your wearable.

watch.text: Repeat the reading tonight and check the cabin temperature.

alert.text: Repeat the reading now. If it stays this far from baseline, follow the mission medical protocol.

name: Resistive exercise
whyItMatters: NASA reports that crews exercise about two hours a day to counter bone and muscle loss in microgravity.
howToMeasure: Minutes of resistive exercise logged today.

watch.text: Add 15 minutes of resistive exercise to your daily session.

alert.text: Return to your baseline resistive exercise time, adding it in steps.

name: Cabin CO2
whyItMatters: The spacecraft is a closed environment, so the air you breathe depends on its life-support system. NASA's standard limits the 1-hour average CO2 partial pressure in the habitable volume to 3 mmHg, and NASA reports that keeping the 7-day average below 2.5 mmHg keeps the risk of headache under 1%.
howToMeasure: Read by the cabin sensor closest to your sleep station.

watch.text: Check airflow at your sleep and work stations.

alert.text: Tell the crew and follow the cabin air protocol.

limit.label: NASA-STD-3001 limit, 1-hour average
limit.note: The standard is a 1-hour average. The tool compares it with the mean of the last 3 daily readings, which is a simplification.

name: Radiation dose
whyItMatters: NASA considers space radiation one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight. Dose adds up over the whole mission.
howToMeasure: Read from your personal dosimeter at the end of the day.

watch.text: Spend more of today in the better-shielded areas of the cabin.

alert.text: Move to the shielded area and follow the radiation protocol.

name: Mood
whyItMatters: NASA describes behavioral responses in crews that live isolated and confined for a long time. A lasting drop in how you rate your own mood is worth a closer look.
howToMeasure: Rate your mood today from 1 (very low) to 5 (very good).

watch.text: Take your scheduled personal time today and talk with a crewmate.

alert.text: Tell a crewmate how you have been feeling and follow the behavioral health protocol.

name: Blood pressure, systolic
whyItMatters: NASA notes that the body's organs must adjust to each new gravity level. A lasting change from your own baseline is worth a closer look.
howToMeasure: Use the cuff after sitting still for five minutes. This is the upper number.

watch.text: Repeat the blood pressure reading after five minutes at rest.

alert.text: Repeat the blood pressure reading now. If it stays this far from baseline, follow the mission medical protocol.

name: Blood pressure, diastolic
whyItMatters: NASA notes that the body's organs must adjust to each new gravity level. A lasting change from your own baseline is worth a closer look.
howToMeasure: Use the cuff after sitting still for five minutes. This is the lower number.

watch.text: Repeat the blood pressure reading after five minutes at rest.

alert.text: Repeat the blood pressure reading now. If it stays this far from baseline, follow the mission medical protocol.

name: Blood sugar
whyItMatters: The challenge names blood sugar as a core health indicator. A lasting change from your own baseline is worth a closer look.

watch.text: Repeat the fasting reading tomorrow and note what you ate today.

alert.text: Repeat the reading now. If it stays this far from baseline, follow the mission medical protocol.

name: Body temperature
whyItMatters: NASA lists temperature among the habitability factors of a closed spacecraft. A lasting change from your own baseline is worth a closer look.
howToMeasure: Use the thermometer at the same time each day.

watch.text: Repeat the temperature reading in an hour.

alert.text: Repeat the temperature reading now. If it stays this far from baseline, follow the mission medical protocol.
